This is apart from the police brutality that happened after the organized dispersal at Mendiola where it resulted in the death of an unidentified civilian and the injury and arrest of 216 individuals, including 89 minors, which were condemned by various human rights groups.

One of the individuals, who was seen being beaten and dragged until he was arrested by state forces, was identified to be Mattheo Wovi Villanueva, a student of the UP Diliman College of Arts and Letters who only served as a security marshal and paralegal to a media personnel during the mobilization. 

Villanueva is currently held at the Manila Police District Headquarters where progressive groups and the victims’ family members staged an indignation protest, last Sept. 22, for the immediate release of detained youth protesters.

Karapatan further criticized the police brutality by comparing yesterday’s events to the unreasonable and excessive force during Marcos Sr.’s Martial Law era in quelling activism and street protests.

As of press time, Karapatan and other progressive organizations join the families of those arrested outside of MPD, flagging the continued delay of the inquest hearings for those warrantlessly arrested in Mendiola during Sunday’s protest, despite official announcements that the inquest would be held today, Sept. 23.

Under Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code, authorities have only 36 hours to bring a warrantless arrest before a court or face arbitrary detention charges.

One of the most famous lines from Cars is Doc Hudson’s advice to Lightning McQueen: “Turn right to go left.”

After spending last week studying racing games, here’s my advice to anyone building in the space:

The only right direction to head in is East. ➡️ 

South East Asia f*ing loves racing games. I know what you're thinking: people in Asia will download anything. But here's the surprising part: with racing, they’re also the ones spending the most. Southeast Asia leads in revenue across racing sub-genres.

And it's not just China and Japan. Countries like Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, and the Philippines now rank among the top spenders in racing games, and not by a small margin. Some games are pulling 40–50% of their revenue from just one or two SEA territories.

Why does SEA pay for racing games you ask?

After doing some digging, here's my best guess:

👾 Arcades built the habit
In the 2000s, malls across Jakarta, Manila, Bangkok were filled with Daytona USA, Initial D, Wangan Midnight. Racing wasn’t just about winning a round; it was about the crowd behind you, the bragging rights, the friends lined up for the next turn. That same social, competitive DNA carried seamlessly into mobile racing clubs and leaderboards.

🏎️ Motorsport is mainstream
The Singapore F1 night race draws ~269k fans each year. Sepang’s MotoGP in Malaysia hit ~185k. Thailand’s Buriram circuit holds 100k. These aren’t side events, they’re national spectacles. With that level of passion around motorsport, spending digitally to race, customize, and flex feels natural.

🚗 Car ownership is aspirational
In cities like Jakarta or Manila, owning a car is out of reach for many: import taxes, congestion, and high costs make it unattainable. Racing games offer the cheapest way to own, tune, and show off a dream garage. Virtual cars scratch an itch that real ones can’t.

🎥 Media & pop culture amplify it
Fast & Furious marathons, Japanese drift culture, local YouTube street-racing vlogs; SEA is steeped in car culture. The stories people consume offline keep virtual racing alive online, making every new car drop or skin feel part of a bigger narrative.

📱 Mobile-first economies scale it
Smartphones + cheap data = the perfect funnel. While the West splits time across PC and consoles, SEA is all-in on mobile. That makes racing games easier to spread, easier to share, and easier to monetize at scale.

💳 Frictionless payments monetize it
GCash in the Philippines, QRIS in Indonesia, GrabPay in Malaysia, MoMo in Vietnam. Micro-spends are as routine as buying lunch. That’s why SEA already leads globally in out-of-app gaming payments. The ecosystem is built for volume.

In conclusion, here is some food for thought:
Yes, your VCs might tell you to build for the US if you want paying users. That’s the default advice.

But if you’re trying to get rich building racing games, maybe you should be thinking Tokyo before Texas.💰 

#games #racinggames #sea #startups
